all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual reality tour
concepts.definition: A virtual reality tour is a virtual reality experience for visiting a recreated place without physically going there, in which movement from one point to another is either user-controlled or system-controlled.

defining_facts.text: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.

Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques.

Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements.

System-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to concentrate more on the experience itself.
Lack of user involvement in system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours makes them less realistic and defeats the purpose of presence because the user is unable to control the movement.

The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

concepts.name: latency
concepts.definition: Latency is the time delay, or time gap, in virtual reality between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

defining_facts.text: Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
In head-mounted display (HMD)-based virtual reality (VR), cybersickness (CS) increases with latency; the more latency there is, the more likely it is to induce cybersickness.
Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

concepts.name: teleportation
concepts.definition: Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.

defining_facts.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

concepts.name: rendering
concepts.definition: Rendering is the multi-stage computational process that creates a scene's visual output as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed, and, in a broad sense, output for other senses.

defining_facts.text: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.
In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses.

From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.
The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and if all rendering-related computations were carried out by the central processing unit (CPU), the CPU's time would be consumed by rendering, leaving it with very little time for other tasks and the system could do little except rendering; to avoid this and increase efficiency, rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component.

The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.

The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

concepts.name: platform
concepts.definition: A platform is the combination of hardware and an operating system.

defining_facts.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.
In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.

A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

concepts.name: computer graphics
concepts.definition: Computer graphics (CG) is the area that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models. It creates or represents objects, synthesizes them into a scene, allows users to manipulate images on a screen, creates the perception of motion, and renders the scene on a display so humans can perceive it.

defining_facts.text: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

For a good virtual reality (VR) immersive experience, client-end hardware is needed to support requirements arising from rendering or computer graphics and to manage rendering or computer graphics related issues, and the complexity required to render a scene corresponds to the need for high-end hardware support.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.
The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: vehicle metaphor
concepts.definition: Vehicle metaphor is a virtual reality user locomotion technique in which a user's avatar boards a vehicle and operates its controls while the user remains seated.

defining_facts.text: A popular option for user locomotion in virtual reality (VR) is operating a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the user's avatar can walk, run, jump, swim, climb, board a vehicle, and operate its controls while the user remains seated; the vehicle option is a vehicle metaphor.

concepts.name: point of interest
concepts.definition: Point of interest (POI) is a significant spot in a virtual tour, modeled as a graph node or vertex with importance and a maximum waiting time, that need not be a physical object and is visited to inspect or interact with objects.

defining_facts.text: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.
In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.
For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.
A point of interest (POI) in the Satra graph does not have to refer to an actual physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are.

When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.
The maximum wait time at a point of interest (POI) is the time a user needs to stop at the point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

concepts.name: three-dimensional graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process of computation that starts from object representation and ends by computing pixel intensities for a pixel-grid display, with five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, a viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.

defining_facts.text: The three-dimensional (3D) computer graphics pipeline (3D graphics pipeline) is a stage-wise process of computation starting from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.
The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer.

Transforming an object definition to a pixel-level scene description in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline uses six coordinate systems: the local coordinate system, the world coordinate system, the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, the device coordinate system, and the pixel-grid or screen coordinate system.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the scan conversion stage, also called the rendering stage, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

concepts.name: Majuli case study
concepts.definition: The Majuli case study is a virtual reality case study focused on designing, implementing, and evaluating an immersive interactive tour that digitally preserves the ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

defining_facts.text: The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

concepts.name: Majuli
concepts.definition: Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in Assam that is surrounded on all sides by the river and its tributaries and is considered the world's largest inhabited river island.

defining_facts.text: Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.

Majuli's monsoon season is typically May to September, its non-monsoon season is October to April, and it has an average annual precipitation of 1704 millimeters, an average maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, and a minimum temperature of 7 degrees Celsius.

Majuli's area was about 1250 square kilometers around 1900, had reduced to about 570 square kilometers in 1975, and had further reduced to about 427 square kilometers by 2021, with 2021 data giving about 427.09 square kilometers, an overall reduction of almost two-thirds and about a 25 percent reduction from 1975 to 2021.

Majuli has been constantly hit by severe annual floods and erosion, and river erosion is consuming the island and reducing its habitable area, so formerly habitable areas are no longer habitable and have become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas.

The severe annual floods and erosion of Majuli endanger its cultural resources and its material existence, and although measures are being taken to prevent further erosion, there is a real possibility that the island may disappear.
Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.

Majuli is home to several tribal communities, including three distinctive tribal communities—Mising, Deori, and Sonowal Kachari—whose distinctive ways of living, rituals, heritage, and culture make them unique.

Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.

Intangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms in music, dance forms, drama or performing arts, mask making, vernacular architecture, weaving, food, and agricultural practices, and it is typically embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.
Majuli also has ecological heritage, consisting of the flora and fauna that exist because of the island's unique geology, geography, and topography from natural formation.
Before Majuli disappears, it is essential to preserve its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage.
Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the state of Assam, surrounded on all sides by the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries.
Satras on Majuli are monasteries of the Vaisnavite faith that contain tangible and intangible cultural aspects, and there are 22 Satras in total.
Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest.
Majuli is the world's largest inhabited river island, located in eastern India on the river Brahmaputra and surrounded by the Brahmaputra and its tributary.

concepts.name: satra
concepts.definition: A Satra is a monastery on Majuli, Assam, that is an authoritative center of the Vaishnavite faith and a living workshop for visual and performing arts.

defining_facts.text: Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.

Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.
Satras on Majuli are monasteries of the Vaisnavite faith that contain tangible and intangible cultural aspects, and there are 22 Satras in total.
Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest.

The Majuli virtual tour contains a large number of geographically spread information points, including satras (Vaishnavite monasteries), villages, tribal villages, towns, and other places of interest, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.

The Majuli multimodal archive consists of regular images, 360-degree images, and videos for the indigenous architectural heritage of satras (Vaishnavite monasteries) and village life, 3D models for landscape and architecture, 2D drone shots for landscape, flora, and fauna, 2D videos for intangible cultural heritage, and textual descriptions.

concepts.name: image
concepts.definition: An image is the whole interface displayed on a computer screen, not only the main object, comprising geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

defining_facts.text: The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

concepts.name: textual description
concepts.definition: A textual description is descriptive text that provides additional context about locations, significant spots, artifacts, objects, or elements in a virtual tour or multimodal archive.

defining_facts.text: The virtual tour system provides textual descriptions of a place as informative notifications and descriptions that provide additional context about locations and significant spots.

concepts.name: navigation technique
concepts.definition: A navigation technique is an interaction technique for moving from one point to another in a virtual world with a change in viewpoint, mostly without object interaction; it is broadly categorized as walking-based, steering-based, selection-based, or manipulation-based.

defining_facts.text: Navigation techniques are interaction techniques for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.

Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques.

concepts.name: video player
concepts.definition: A video player is a part of a virtual tablet interface in a virtual tour that lets users view cultural or ecological videos relevant to their current location, including 360-degree, drone, or 2D videos, with a volume controller and other controls.

defining_facts.text: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.
The video player in the virtual tablet interface has a volume controller and other controls and is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place.

In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

concepts.name: resource optimization
concepts.definition: Resource optimization is the technological optimization of resource requirements in extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR), that minimizes those requirements while maximizing immersive experience without compromising it. It generally focuses on client-end hardware so users can have a good experience with affordable hardware.

defining_facts.text: Optimization in virtual reality (VR) can be considered from two perspectives: optimized experience, that is, psychophysiological experience optimization, and optimized resource utilization or resource requirement, that is, technological optimization; these requirements are present in any extended reality (XR) system, but they gain more prominence in an immersive experience.

In virtual reality (VR), effective resource optimization means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience, without compromising it and, to the extent possible, without reducing its quality; this requires balancing the trade-offs between resource requirements and experience.
The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience.

Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

never_defined.name: handheld controller
never_defined.definition: A handheld controller is an input device held by the user, used in non-immersive VR, and an example of a self-grounded haptic device.

never_defined.name: real time
never_defined.definition: Real time is a condition in which interactions are reflected immediately and content loading has minimal latency.

never_defined.name: smartphone
never_defined.definition: A smartphone is a familiar handheld device used for augmented reality; when placed in a cardboard virtual reality headset, it displays stereoscopic views, and it can also serve as the processing element of a virtual reality system.

never_defined.name: stereoscopic view
never_defined.definition: A stereoscopic view is a view displayed by a smartphone in a virtual reality headset to provide an immersive environment.

never_defined.name: processor
never_defined.definition: Processor is one of the three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system.

never_defined.name: computational requirement
never_defined.definition: Computational requirement is the amount of computation needed for tracking or rendering, and it is higher for larger environments or rich interactive multimodal content.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional model
never_defined.definition: A three-dimensional model is a model of objects, structures, or environments used in virtual reality tours and augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: memory
never_defined.definition: Memory is part of the hardware in typical virtual reality systems and standalone computing devices.

never_defined.name: animation
never_defined.definition: Animation is computer graphics content or an asset used for creating the perception of motion and in representing objects or complex characters.

never_defined.name: size
never_defined.definition: Size is a property of virtual objects or a measure of virtual reality applications, appearing in perception, object selection, modeling, and storage optimization.

never_defined.name: video
never_defined.definition: Video is one of the items in a virtual reality multimedia archive, where it may be 360-degree, drone, or regular two-dimensional content and is used to provide location-relevant cultural or ecological information.

never_defined.name: 360-degree image
never_defined.definition: A 360-degree image is a captured image of a place used to model places and to move from one point to another in a virtual reality tour.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional drone shot
never_defined.definition: A two-dimensional drone shot is a part of a multimodal heritage archive used to showcase the landscape, top view, flora, and fauna of locations and to preserve cultural and ecological heritage.

never_defined.name: Majuli virtual reality system
never_defined.definition: The Majuli virtual reality system is an immersive virtual reality experience that has a full version and a compressed mobile version.

never_defined.name: gigabyte
never_defined.definition: Gigabyte (GB) is used to express the size of an application or system.

never_defined.name: cloud
never_defined.definition: Cloud is a service that stores videos and is used to load them when requested, reducing local storage, data-access, and computational requirements.

never_defined.name: video thumbnail
never_defined.definition: A Video thumbnail is a selectable part of a video player used to load a video.

never_defined.name: client device
never_defined.definition: A client device is a device on which an application is deployed and on which videos can be stored, rather than in cloud services.

never_defined.name: video playback
never_defined.definition: Video playback is a feature of a virtual reality system that can be removed to reduce storage requirements and make the experience less realistic, or retained using cloud-based services.

never_defined.name: Majuli virtual tour
never_defined.definition: The Majuli virtual tour is a virtual tour that contains many geographically spread information points and uses walking within each point and teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between points to present rich multimodal content.

never_defined.name: optimization
never_defined.definition: Optimization is the balancing of psychophysiological experience and resource utilization in an extended reality system so that immersive experience is maximized while resource requirements and cybersickness are minimized.

never_defined.name: walking
never_defined.definition: Walking is a navigation technique used within an information point.

never_defined.name: regular image
never_defined.definition: A regular image is one of the image types in a multimodal archive.

never_defined.name: multimodal content
never_defined.definition: Multimodal content is content in an application that includes several different media types.

never_defined.name: static image
never_defined.definition: A static image is a simple image whose rendering involves lower computational requirements than rendering rich interactive multimodal content.

never_defined.name: storage and retrieval support
never_defined.definition: Storage and retrieval support is fast support required for real-time realistic interactive rendering of rich, interactively changeable multimodal content.

never_defined.name: real-time interactive rendering
never_defined.definition: Real-time interactive rendering is the rendering of rich multimodal content that can be interactively changed, including videos and animations, and it requires fast storage and retrieval support and has a high computational requirement.

never_defined.name: tethered
never_defined.definition: Tethered is a connection to a fixed computer that a standalone computing device does not need.

never_defined.name: fixed computer
never_defined.definition: A fixed computer is a computer that a standalone computing device does not need to be tethered to.

never_defined.name: high-end graphics workstation
never_defined.definition: A High-end graphics workstation is a high-end platform with good graphics processing unit (GPU) support that is typically used for render pipelines requiring a good amount of resources.

never_defined.name: computing power
never_defined.definition: Computing power is a quantity that a device has, and when it is lower, an application may require optimization to reduce computations and memory access.

never_defined.name: storage
never_defined.definition: Storage is the space in an XR system required to store data, and it can be reduced by storing data in the cloud rather than locally.

never_defined.name: application
never_defined.definition: An application is the top layer in a Unity layered architecture.

never_defined.name: computation
never_defined.definition: Computation is an application-related activity, including memory access, that can be reduced by reducing the application's size.

never_defined.name: memory access
never_defined.definition: Memory access is an associated computation of an application that is reduced when the application's size and rendering requirements are reduced.

never_defined.name: rendering requirement
never_defined.definition: A rendering requirement is a requirement that is reduced, along with associated memory access, when the size of an application is reduced.

never_defined.name: cloud computing
never_defined.definition: Cloud computing is a computing concept used in scalable and affordable extended reality systems for resource optimization, with videos stored in the cloud and loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally.

never_defined.name: data-access requirement
never_defined.definition: A Data-access requirement is a requirement that can be reduced by loading data from the cloud rather than storing it locally.

never_defined.name: computational reduction
never_defined.definition: Computational reduction is a reduction in computation that corresponds to a reduced application size on a client device.

never_defined.name: cloud server
never_defined.definition: A cloud server is a server that a cloud-based video-loading optimization relies on to load high-quality videos in real time.

never_defined.name: bandwidth
never_defined.definition: Bandwidth is a requirement, together with network coverage and minimal latency, for cloud-based video-loading optimization to load high-quality videos in real time.

never_defined.name: network coverage
never_defined.definition: Network coverage is a network connectivity requirement, together with high bandwidth and minimal latency, for cloud-based video-loading optimization to load high-quality videos in real time.

never_defined.name: network connectivity
never_defined.definition: Network connectivity is a requirement for cloud-based video-loading optimization, involving high bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time.

never_defined.name: optimization strategy
never_defined.definition: An optimization strategy is used to adapt a virtual reality system deployment when the full system's size and associated computation exceed what average smartphones typically support, for example by compressing images and removing video playback support.

never_defined.name: image compression
never_defined.definition: Image compression is an optimization technique used to reduce the storage requirements of images and address computational issues in immersive experiences.

never_defined.name: storage requirement
never_defined.definition: Storage requirement is a virtual-reality system requirement that can be reduced by compressing images and removing video playback support.

never_defined.name: cloud-based service
never_defined.definition: A Cloud-based service is one of the approaches to address computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences, and it could allow video playback to be retained.

never_defined.name: compression technique
never_defined.definition: Compression technique is one of the approaches to address computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences.

never_defined.name: device
never_defined.definition: A device is used to run and deploy immersive virtual reality and marker-based AR applications, receive builds over USB, and perform rendering.
